title: Paul and Barnabas split (Acts 15:36–41)
hook: a sharp disagreement over young Mark; later Paul calls Mark useful
tomorrow: Paul dreams of a man in Macedonia. who's waiting when he lands?

segments.voice: Yesterday a long argument ended in a letter: it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us. Seemed good to the Holy Spirit. The two men who carried that letter are about to have an argument of their own.
screen: `SEEMED GOOD TO THE HOLY SPIRIT.` → `NOW, THEIR OWN ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: Planning a road trip is the easy part. The fight starts over who gets a seat in the car. Antioch, not long after the council. Paul says to Barnabas: "Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do." Barnabas is in, and he wants to bring young John Mark. Paul says no. Not him. Not the one who left last time. Two friends who stood side by side in front of crowds and councils are now standing face to face, and neither one is backing down.
screen: `WHO GETS A SEAT IN THE CAR?` → `LET US GO AGAIN.` → `NOT JOHN MARK.`

segments.voice: Paul's reason is right there in the text. Mark is the one "who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work." Barnabas, whose name Acts once explained as "The son of consolation," wants to give him another chance. A later letter calls Mark "sister's son to Barnabas," so this is family, too. Both men have a point. Paul is thinking about the road and the work ahead; Barnabas is thinking about the young man in front of him. And Acts doesn't tidy it up: "the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other." Barnabas takes Mark and sails for Cyprus. Paul chooses Silas and goes by land. Acts never says who was right. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight, and it's outside Acts. Letters that carry Paul's name mention Mark later, warmly. One counts him among Paul's fellow workers. Another says: "Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry." Tradition takes him to be the same Mark. If so, the young man Paul wouldn't travel with became the one he asked for by name. The split was real. So, it seems, was the mending. Neither one cancels the other.
screen: `HE WENT NOT WITH THEM.` · `THE SON OF CONSOLATION.` · `THEY DEPARTED ASUNDER.` · `PROFITABLE TO ME.` · then, large: `THEY PARTED, AND LATER MENDED.`

segments.voice: Grab a pen and any scrap of paper. Write the first name of someone you parted from badly, and beside it one word you'd still wish them: peace, rest, luck, anything true. Nothing needs sending or fixing; if you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Paul and Barnabas split. A sharp disagreement over John Mark, and two journeys instead of one.
Pocket this one: they parted, and later mended, and Paul asked for Mark by name. Go gently.

chat.meaning: Acts tells a sharp split; later letters have Paul asking for Mark and calling him profitable. Parted now doesn't have to mean parted for good.

John Mark.meaning: a young helper who left the team at Pamphylia

Pamphylia.meaning: a region on the south coast of what is now Turkey

Barnabas.meaning: Paul's partner; Acts says the name means son of consolation

Silas.meaning: the companion Paul chose after the split

notes: 'Letters that carry Paul's name' is worded on purpose: scholars differ on who wrote Colossians and 2 Timothy. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with this.
That the Mark of Colossians 4:10, Philemon 24 and 2 Timothy 4:11 is John Mark of Acts is attributed to tradition. Confirm.
Colossians 4:10 KJV 'sister's son to Barnabas'; newer translations read 'cousin'. The lesson quotes the KJV and says only 'family'.
'The son of consolation' is Acts 4:36's own interpretation of Barnabas's name, not a claim of the lesson.
